doc.title: Lou Pallo interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 14, 2007

title: Strings thrill, Al Caiola with the symphony, studio expectations
summary: Pallo recalls the thrill of strings, playing with Al Caiola and Doc Severinsen conducting the Washington orchestra, and the time pressure in the studio.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: Session players on the hits: "I played on that record"

blocks.x: And then just from the experience of the strings, what a chill down my spine listening to them right in front of you. It was a first experience with the strings, oh fabulous.
Yeah I know, I’ve had that feeling too, like oh I want to get this right.

And then of course I jumped from there to when I was with Al Caiola we did the Washington Symphony Orchestra with Doc Severinsen conducting. That was, that’s a hundred pieces, is it a hundred pieces, or ninety-something piece orchestra. That was a thrill, being out front with Al, Al was on my left, I’m here, and we had an accordionist and Doc Severinsen in front of us conducting the symphony behind us. Oh, hearing those strings behind me. It was — I loved it, loved it.
In the studio, those kinds of sessions, they expect you to do it correctly the first time if possible?
Because it’s a time thing, right?
And they don’t want to have overtime.
Do you recall if Petula Clark was even there?
No she wasn’t there. We were doing the rhythm.
The tracks for the rhythm section. And with not only rhythm, I’m sorry, the whole music background.
Do you remember what the song was? Was it one of her hits?
It was an original and I think “Born Free” might have been one of them. I’m not too sure. “Born Free,” oh I can’t think of the other one.
